title: Arms and the man
src: Virgil, Aeneid I.1–7 · tr. J. W. Mackail (1885)
author: Virgil
lines: I sing of arms and the man who of old from the coasts of Troy came,
an exile of fate, to Italy and the shore of Lavinium;
hard driven on land and on the deep by the violence of heaven,
for cruel Juno's unforgetful anger,
and hard bestead in war also,
ere he might found a city and carry his gods into Latium;
from whom is the Latin race, the lords of Alba,
and the stately city Rome.
why: The first sentence of Rome's great poem, and one of the most famous openings in literature. It tells the whole story in a breath: a refugee who loses everything, carries what is sacred with him, suffers on land and sea, and founds something greater than himself. Say it when a task feels larger than you are.

title: Hand to the plough
author: Luke
lines: But Jesus said to him,
“No one, having put his hand to the plow,
and looking back,
is fit for God’s Kingdom.”
why: Jesus's answer to a man who wanted to follow him, but first to say goodbye at home. A ploughman who looks over his shoulder ploughs a crooked furrow. Some callings ask everything, and cannot be done half-turned. Say it when you have chosen something good and feel the pull to look back.

title: True law is right reason
src: Cicero, On the Commonwealth III.33 · tr. Francis Barham (1841), revised by C. D. Yonge (1853)
author: Cicero
work: On the Commonwealth III.33 (preserved by Lactantius, Institutes VI.8)
translator: Francis Barham (1841), revised by C. D. Yonge (1853)
lines: True law is right reason conformable to nature,
universal, unchangeable, eternal,
whose commands urge us to duty,
and whose prohibitions restrain us from evil.
It is not one thing at Rome, and another at Athens;
one thing to-day, and another to-morrow;
but in all times and nations this universal law must forever reign,
eternal and imperishable.
why: Cicero's definition of natural law: there is a justice above every government, the same for every people, which no senate or vote can repeal. It runs from here through the Church Fathers and Aquinas to the modern idea of human rights. Say it when someone tells you that right and wrong are only what a country happens to decide.

title: To give every man his due
src: Justinian, Institutes I.1 · tr. J. B. Moyle (1883; 5th ed. 1913)
author: Justinian
lines: Justice is the set and constant purpose
which gives to every man his due.
The precepts of the law are these:
to live honestly, to injure no one,
and to give every man his due.
why: The first words a law student read in the Roman Empire, and for a thousand years after in the universities of Europe. Justice is not a feeling but a settled will, and its test is simple: what does this person rightly have a claim to? Say it before you settle a quarrel, mark a piece of work or pay a bill.
